items.stem: State what happens to the vapour inside the condenser.
items.modelAnswer: It cools and condenses into the pure liquid, which collects in a beaker.

items.stem: State which liquid boils first when fractionally distilling ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (boiling point 100 °C).
items.modelAnswer: Ethanol — heat the mixture to the lowest boiling point present, and that substance boils first and distils out.

items.stem: Explain why heating stops when the thermometer reaches 100 °C during the fractional distillation of ethanol and water.
items.modelAnswer: Because 100 °C is water's boiling point — collecting past it would distil water instead of the ethanol, which comes over at 78 °C.

items.stem: A student has propanol (boiling point 97 °C) mixed with ethanol (boiling point 78 °C). State which liquid distils first, and at what thermometer reading it comes over.
items.modelAnswer: Ethanol distils first — heat the mixture to the lowest boiling point present, and that substance boils first — so the ethanol comes over at 78 °C.

items.stem: State the names for the liquid that passes through the filter paper and the solid left on it.
items.modelAnswer: The liquid that passes through is the filtrate; the solid left on the paper is the residue.

items.stem: State what paper chromatography separates, and how.
items.modelAnswer: Dissolved substances, by the different distances they travel with a solvent up the paper.

items.stem: Explain why crystallisation works for a solid whose solubility falls as the hot solution cools.
items.modelAnswer: Because the hot solution holds a lot of dissolved solid; as it cools the solubility falls, the solution can hold less, and the excess solid forms crystals.

items.stem: Two dyes are placed on the same chromatography paper. Dye A is more soluble in the solvent than dye B. State which dye travels further up the paper.
items.modelAnswer: Dye A — more soluble substances travel further up the paper (the pencil line stays above the solvent level throughout the run).

items.stem: State what a pure substance produces on a chromatogram, and what an impure sample produces.
items.modelAnswer: A pure substance produces one spot; an impure sample produces more than one.

items.stem: State what a mixture shows on the chromatography paper.
items.modelAnswer: It separates, showing each of its components as a separate spot.

items.stem: Explain why matching is done by horizontal alignment of dots in a black-and-white exam chromatogram.
items.modelAnswer: Because exam chromatograms are black and white, colour cannot identify anything — dots that line up horizontally (sit at the same height) mark the same substance.

items.stem: A food dye's chromatogram shows two spots. State whether the dye is pure or a mixture.
items.modelAnswer: A mixture — more than one spot means the sample is impure (a mixture of components); a pure substance gives one spot.

items.stem: State the three properties of an Rf value.
items.modelAnswer: It is a ratio, it carries no units, and it always stays below one.

items.stem: State what exam mark schemes reward in Rf measurements.
items.modelAnswer: Careful ruler work on both distances — measured from the baseline to the centre of each dot or front.

items.stem: Explain why an Rf value can never reach one or go above it.
items.modelAnswer: Because the substance never travels further than the solvent front — its distance is divided by the larger solvent distance, so the ratio stays below one.

items.stem: An unknown dye gives Rf = 0.52 in solvent X; the data table lists dye P at 0.52 and dye Q at 0.31 in solvent X. State which dye the unknown likely is, and how to confirm it.
items.modelAnswer: Dye P — measured Rf values compared with tables of known values identify the components of a mixture; run the known dye alongside on the same paper and check the spots line up.

items.stem: State what must be drawn on the paper before any distances are measured.
items.modelAnswer: A solvent front line, drawn at the wet edge (distances are then measured in mm).

items.stem: State the two preparations made before the solvent is poured in.
items.modelAnswer: A pencil start line is drawn 2 cm from the bottom edge of the paper, and each colouring is spotted with its own capillary tube in spots no bigger than 2-3 mm.

items.stem: Explain why sharing one capillary tube between two colourings would spoil the results.
items.modelAnswer: Because each colouring gets its own capillary tube so one sample cannot contaminate another — a shared tube would mix the samples, and the spots would no longer be each dye's own.

items.stem: After an hour a student's solvent front has climbed only halfway up the paper. State what they should do, and why.
items.modelAnswer: Keep the run going — leave it undisturbed until the solvent has climbed at least three quarters of the paper (lifting it before the front reaches the top).

items.stem: State what happens to ink start lines in the solvent, and what is used instead.
items.modelAnswer: Ink start lines dissolve and run with the solvent, so every line and label is drawn in pencil.

items.stem: State the timing rule for lifting the paper out of the beaker.
items.modelAnswer: The paper comes out before the solvent front reaches the top, or Rf cannot be calculated.

items.stem: Explain why solvent poured above the start line spoils the chromatogram.
items.modelAnswer: Because solvent above the start line dissolves the samples away into the pool of solvent, so no dye ever climbs the paper.

items.stem: Spot U matches colouring B's Rf exactly, but U also shows a second spot that matches nothing in the table. State what U contains.
items.modelAnswer: U contains dye B plus at least one other dye — matching Rf values mean the unknown holds that same dye (backed up by a visual check), and the extra unmatched spot is another component, so U is a mixture.

items.stem: State the three kinds of sub-atomic particle inside an atom.
items.modelAnswer: Protons, neutrons and electrons.

items.stem: State the path electrons take around the nucleus.
items.modelAnswer: Electrons race around the nucleus along orbital paths known as shells.

items.stem: Explain why an atom's mass is effectively all contained in its nucleus.
items.modelAnswer: Because a proton and a neutron each have relative mass 1, while an electron's mass of about 1/1840 is treated as negligible — so effectively all of an atom's mass sits in its nucleus, where the protons and neutrons are.

items.stem: A particle diagram shows two hydrogen atoms joined chemically to one oxygen atom. State whether the particle shown is an atom or a molecule, and why.
items.modelAnswer: A molecule — a molecule is two or more atoms joined chemically, and this particle joins three atoms.

items.stem: State how the number of neutrons in an atom is found.
items.modelAnswer: Take the atomic number away from the mass number (neutrons = mass number − atomic number).

items.stem: State the particle counts for lithium (atomic number 3, mass number 7).
items.modelAnswer: 3 protons, 3 electrons and 4 neutrons.

items.stem: Explain why an atom's atomic number also tells you its electron count.
items.modelAnswer: Because in a neutral atom the electrons equal the protons — the atomic number counts protons in the nucleus, and in a neutral atom it counts the electrons too.

items.stem: Atom X and atom Y both carry 17 protons; X holds 18 neutrons and Y holds 20. State the relationship between X and Y.
items.modelAnswer: They are isotopes — isotopes share an element and proton count but differ in their neutron counts.

items.stem: State the term each isotope contributes to the relative-atomic-mass equation.
items.modelAnswer: Percentage abundance times mass number — each isotope contributes one term.

items.stem: State where an element's Ar value sits relative to its isotope mass numbers.
items.modelAnswer: In between — Ar is a weighted average, so it sits between the isotope mass numbers.

items.stem: Explain why the relative-atomic-mass equation divides the summed terms by 100.
items.modelAnswer: Because the abundances are percentages — dividing by 100 converts the percentage-weighted total back to an average per atom.

items.stem: Chlorine has two stable isotopes: 75% of mass 35 and 25% of mass 37. State the top line of the Ar calculation for chlorine.
items.modelAnswer: (75 x 35) + (25 x 37) — each isotope contributes one term of percentage abundance times mass number.

items.stem: State the rounding rule of record for relative-atomic-mass working.
items.modelAnswer: Keep full precision through the working and round only in the final line.

items.stem: State the two products added in the rubidium top line, and their sum.
items.modelAnswer: 6120 and 2436, which sum to 8556.

items.stem: Explain why the rubidium sample's Ar (85.6) sits closer to 85 than to 87.
items.modelAnswer: Because Ar is a weighted average — the 72% abundance of the mass-85 isotope outweighs the 28% of mass-87, so the average sits between the mass numbers but nearer the more abundant isotope.

items.stem: A different rubidium-like sample holds 60% of mass 85 and 40% of mass 87. Predict whether its Ar sits above or below 86.0.
items.modelAnswer: Below 86.0 — more of the lighter isotope (60% of mass 85) pulls the weighted average below the 50-50 midpoint of 86.0.

items.stem: State how many elements have been isolated and identified so far.
items.modelAnswer: Over 100 elements.

items.stem: State the number that acts as an element's fingerprint.
items.modelAnswer: The atomic number — it never changes, even in reactions.

items.stem: Explain why moving one element to the right along the table always adds exactly one proton.
items.modelAnswer: Because elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, and the atomic number counts protons — so each element carries one proton more than the element before it.

items.stem: Elements A and B sit in the same column of the periodic table. Predict how their chemical properties compare.
items.modelAnswer: They are similar — ordering by atomic number places elements with similar properties in the same columns.

items.stem: State the two numbers an atom's position in the table gives you, and what each counts.
items.modelAnswer: The period number gives the number of electron shells an atom holds, and the group number gives the number of electrons in the outermost shell.

items.stem: State the exception in how the table's columns are numbered.
items.modelAnswer: The final column is named Group 0 instead of Group 8 (groups run 1 to 7).

items.stem: Explain what the period number of an element records about its atoms.
items.modelAnswer: It records the number of electron shells an atom holds — a Period 2 element has two shells.

items.stem: An element sits in Group 5. State how many electrons it holds in its outermost shell.
items.modelAnswer: Five — the group number gives the number of electrons in the outermost shell.
